# RDD audit checklist (v0.15, generated by scripts/skillgen)

23 checks. Each rests on claims from the methods literature, and each one points to where to read more. The 25 sources listed under **Sources** below are the ones cited in the further-reading lines.

**How to read a verdict.** `PASS` / `FLAG` are decided by the stated conditions. `NA` means the check is out of scope for this design - never that the paper was silent. When a check applies and the paper says nothing, the verdict is the one given in *When silent*.

**Evidence scope.** A verdict covers only the text the audit could see. A FLAG on material the paper says is in an appendix or replication package means "not shown here", not "not done" - such flags carry that caveat in the report.

**Thresholds are rules of thumb unless marked otherwise.** Where a cutoff is conventional rather than derived, the item says so, and near-threshold values are reported as borderline rather than silently rounded to a verdict.

## Scope triggers

A check applies only when its scope trigger fires. Triggers key on the paper's own explicit stance and default OUT when the paper is silent.

- **`all`** - Every design the paper itself calls a regression-discontinuity (RD/RDD) design, i.e. it states that treatment is assigned by whether a running/forcing/assignment score crosses a fixed cutoff. Fires on the paper's own RD self-description; a paper that never claims an RD/threshold design is out of module.
- **`covariate_adjusted`** - Fires only when the paper states it adds covariates to the RD estimating specification or otherwise conditions its point estimate on covariates. Near-miss that does NOT fire: reporting covariate balance purely as a diagnostic while the headline estimate is unadjusted.
- **`fuzzy_rd`** - Fires only when the paper states its design is fuzzy / has imperfect compliance at the cutoff (the probability of treatment jumps by less than one, or it instruments received treatment with the cutoff indicator). Near-miss that does NOT fire: a sharp design the paper describes as perfect/deterministic compliance; using an instrumental variable elsewhere in the paper unrelated to the cutoff.
- **`fuzzy`** - Fires only when the paper itself describes its design as fuzzy: it states that treatment take-up changes probabilistically (not deterministically) at the cutoff, or that it uses the cutoff/assignment indicator as an instrument for treatment actually received. NOT fired by: a sharp design that mentions occasional non-compliance in passing, or a paper that merely reports imperfect data coverage. If the paper never declares probabilistic take-up or an instrumenting step, the design is out of scope (NA).
- **`pcrd`** - Fires only when the paper defines its RD treatment as a predetermined characteristic of the winning unit/candidate (a politician-characteristic RD), so the contrast is winners of differing types. Near-miss that does NOT fire: a standard party- or incumbency-status close-election RD where treatment is which party/incumbent won, not a candidate trait.
- **`local_poly_datadriven`** - Fires only when the paper states it estimates the RD effect with local polynomial (local linear/quadratic) regression using a data-driven bandwidth it names (MSE-optimal, CER-optimal, cross-validated, or a plug-in selector). Near-miss that does NOT fire: a global polynomial fit over the full range with no bandwidth; a single ad hoc window the paper picks without naming a data-driven selector.
- **`clustered`** - Fires only when the paper states its observation structure is grouped or repeated (multiple observations per unit, a panel of repeated events, or an explicit clustering/grouping level). Keys on the declared data structure, not on whether cluster-robust errors were used. NOT fired by: a single cross-section with one observation per unit. Ambiguous cases are NA.
- **`discrete_rv`** - Fires only when the paper states its running variable is discrete or has few mass points (integer counts, coarse bins). Near-miss that does NOT fire: a continuous running variable rounded only for display; a continuous variable with many distinct values.
- **`geographic_rd`** - Fires only when the paper states it uses a geographic/boundary RD with a spatial (two-dimensional) score or distance-to-a-border running variable. Near-miss that does NOT fire: a one-dimensional non-spatial score; a design that merely includes region fixed effects.
- **`multiple_tests`** - Fires only when the paper reports a battery of several covariate-balance, placebo, or multiple-outcome tests (its own stated set of two or more such tests). Near-miss that does NOT fire: a single balance test or a single outcome.
- **`heaped_rv`** - Fires only when the paper states its running variable heaps/bunches at particular (e.g. round) values. Near-miss that does NOT fire: a smooth continuous density with no reported heaping.

## IDENT

*Identification - the assumptions the causal claim rests on.*

### RDD-IDENT-01 - The paper must justify the RD design with a substantive argument that precise sorting at the cutoff is implausible.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should explain how the score that decides treatment (the running variable) is produced and argue why units could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they land on.

**Why it matters:** The design is credible only if units could not place themselves on the side of the cutoff they preferred.

**Check:** Whether the paper gives a substantive account of how the running variable is generated and why precise sorting around the cutoff is implausible in this setting.

- **Pass:** The paper describes the score-generating mechanism and states a reason (institutional, timing, or informational) that units cannot finely control which side of the cutoff they land on.
- **Flag:** The paper invokes the RD design but offers no substantive argument about the assignment mechanism or the possibility of precise sorting.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Devin Caughey & Jasjeet S. Sekhon. (2011). Elections and the Regression Discontinuity Design: Lessons from Close U.S. House Races, 1942–2008. Political Analysis, 19(4), 385-408. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr032 - p. 405
  - Andrew C. Eggers, Anthony Fowler, Jens Hainmueller, Andrew B. Hall, & James M. Snyder. (2014). On the Validity of the Regression Discontinuity Design for Estimating Electoral Effects: New Evidence from Over 40,000 Close Races. American Journal of Political Science, 59(1), 259-274. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12127 - p. 270
  - David S. Lee & Thomas Lemieux. (2009). Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics. National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w14723 - p. 13
  - David S. Lee & Thomas Lemieux. (2010). Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics. Journal of Economic Literature, 48(2), 281-355. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.48.2.281 - p. 295

### RDD-IDENT-02 - The paper must not adjust for covariates that could themselves have been affected by treatment.

**Scope:** `covariate_adjusted` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should control only for variables that were fixed or measured before treatment was assigned.

**Why it matters:** A control that the treatment could have changed can distort the estimated effect at the cutoff.

**Check:** For each covariate entered into the estimating specification, whether the paper indicates it was determined prior to treatment.

- **Pass:** Every covariate the paper controls for is identified as predetermined (measured or fixed before treatment assignment).
- **Flag:** The paper controls for a covariate that is realized after, or could be affected by, treatment.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Nicolás Idrobo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2019). A Practical Introduction to Regression Discontinuity Designs. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108684606 - p. 78
  - Andrew B. Hall. (2015). What Happens When Extremists Win Primaries?. American Political Science Review, 109(1), 18-42. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055414000641 - p. 21
  - Per Pettersson‐Lidbom. (2008). Do Parties Matter for Economic Outcomes? A Regression-Discontinuity Approach. Journal of the European Economic Association, 6(5), 1037-1056. https://doi.org/10.1162/jeea.2008.6.5.1037 - p. 1041

### RDD-IDENT-03 - The paper must report at least one balance/falsification test (in a table or figure) showing a predetermined variable does not jump at the cutoff.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources) · **Disputed** - Lee (2010) argues that in age/time-based RD designs, covariate-smoothness balance tests are generally uninformative because pre-threshold characteristics are identical by construction, so the required check does not help in that common design class.

**In plain words:** The paper should report, in a table or figure, at least one test showing that a variable set before treatment, such as a baseline characteristic or an earlier value of the outcome, score, or treatment, does not jump at the cutoff.

**Why it matters:** If the design is valid, variables the treatment could not have affected should show no jump at the cutoff.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports falsification tests for a discontinuity at the cutoff in one or more qualifying predetermined variables. Qualifying variables (sourced from the corpus): pre-treatment/baseline covariates, lagged values of the outcome, lagged values of the running variable, and lagged values of the treatment.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a test for a cutoff discontinuity in at least one qualifying predetermined variable and interprets the expected result as no discontinuity.
- **Flag:** The paper reports no balance/placebo test on any predetermined covariate or pre-treatment outcome.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - John DiNardo & David Lee. (2004). Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984-2001. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 119(4), 1383-1441. https://doi.org/10.1162/0033553042476189 - pp. 1412, 1416
  - Jessica Trounstine. (2011). Evidence of a Local Incumbency Advantage. Legislative Studies Quarterly, 36(2), 255-280. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-9162.2011.00013.x - p. 260
  - David S. Lee & Thomas Lemieux. (2010). Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics. Journal of Economic Literature, 48(2), 281-355. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.48.2.281 - p. 334

### RDD-IDENT-04 - The paper must rule out, or explicitly acknowledge, other treatments changing at the same cutoff.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should say whether any other policy or change switches at the same cutoff, and either argue the estimate reflects its treatment or define the effect as the combined bundle.

**Why it matters:** Anything else that changes at the same cutoff gets mixed into the estimate.

**Check:** Whether the paper discusses whether any treatment, policy, or institutional change other than the one of interest occurs at the same cutoff value.

- **Pass:** The paper states whether other interventions coincide at the cutoff and argues the estimate reflects the treatment of interest (or defines the estimand as the bundle).
- **Flag:** The paper never considers whether other changes occur at the cutoff and attributes the discontinuity solely to its treatment.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Fernanda Brollo, Tommaso Nannicini, Roberto Perotti, & Guido Tabellini. (2013). The Political Resource Curse. American Economic Review, 103(5), 1759-1796. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.103.5.1759 - p. 1778
  - Guido W. Imbens & Thomas Lemieux. (2007). Regression discontinuity designs: A guide to practice. Journal of Econometrics, 142(2), 615-635. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.001 - p. 641
  - Luke Keele & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Geographic Boundaries as Regression Discontinuities. Political Analysis, 23(1), 127-155. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu014 - p. 133

### RDD-IDENT-05 - The paper must not claim covariate adjustment repairs a failed identification or balance assumption.

**Scope:** `covariate_adjusted` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should present adding control variables as a way to gain precision or check robustness, not as a fix for a failed balance or design assumption.

**Why it matters:** Adding controls may sharpen the estimate, but it cannot repair a failed assumption that units just either side of the cutoff are comparable (balance or continuity).

**Check:** Whether the paper claims that adding covariates fixes detected imbalance or restores identification.

- **Pass:** The paper treats covariate adjustment as an efficiency or robustness step, not as a remedy for failed identification.
- **Flag:** The paper reports imbalance or a continuity concern and asserts that covariate adjustment resolves it and restores a valid estimate.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Sebastián Calónico, Matias D. Cattaneo, Max H. Farrell, & Rocío Titiunik. (2018). Regression Discontinuity Designs Using Covariates. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 101(3), 442-451. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_00760 - p. 443
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Nicolás Idrobo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2019). A Practical Introduction to Regression Discontinuity Designs. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108684606 - p. 78
  - Devin Caughey & Jasjeet S. Sekhon. (2011). Elections and the Regression Discontinuity Design: Lessons from Close U.S. House Races, 1942–2008. Political Analysis, 19(4), 385-408. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr032 - p. 401

### RDD-IDENT-06 - A fuzzy-RD paper must document the first-stage jump in treatment probability at the cutoff.

**Scope:** `fuzzy_rd` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** In a fuzzy design, where crossing the cutoff raises the chance of treatment rather than fully deciding it, the paper should show the jump in treatment probability at the cutoff, as a figure, estimate, or first-stage coefficient.

**Why it matters:** The design works only if the probability of receiving treatment actually jumps at the cutoff.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports the first-stage effect of crossing the cutoff on treatment receipt (a jump in treatment probability).

- **Pass:** The paper reports the first-stage discontinuity in treatment probability at the cutoff (a figure, estimate, or first-stage coefficient).
- **Flag:** The paper declares a fuzzy design but never demonstrates that treatment receipt changes at the cutoff.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Fernanda Brollo, Tommaso Nannicini, Roberto Perotti, & Guido Tabellini. (2013). The Political Resource Curse. American Economic Review, 103(5), 1759-1796. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.103.5.1759 - p. 1777
  - David S. Lee & Thomas Lemieux. (2010). Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics. Journal of Economic Literature, 48(2), 281-355. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.48.2.281 - p. 305

### RDD-IDENT-07 - A fuzzy-RD paper must state and justify the monotonicity (no-defiers) assumption.

**Scope:** `fuzzy` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** In a fuzzy design, where crossing the cutoff raises the chance of treatment rather than fully deciding it, the paper should state and defend monotonicity: crossing the cutoff never pushes any unit away from treatment.

**Why it matters:** Reading the estimate as a causal effect requires that crossing the cutoff moves treatment in only one direction.

**Check:** Whether the paper states and gives a substantive argument for the monotonicity / no-defiers assumption at the cutoff. A coder decides fired-vs-not from whether the paper declares a fuzzy design; a fired trigger on a paper silent about monotonicity takes verdict_when_silent, and an unfired or ambiguous trigger is NA.

- **Pass:** The paper declares a fuzzy design and states and defends monotonicity (no defiers) at the cutoff.
- **Flag:** The paper declares a fuzzy design but never states or justifies monotonicity.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Fernanda Brollo, Tommaso Nannicini, Roberto Perotti, & Guido Tabellini. (2013). The Political Resource Curse. American Economic Review, 103(5), 1759-1796. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.103.5.1759 - p. 1779
  - David S. Lee & Thomas Lemieux. (2010). Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics. Journal of Economic Literature, 48(2), 281-355. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.48.2.281 - p. 305

### RDD-IDENT-08 - A fuzzy-RD paper must invoke both the exclusion restriction and monotonicity to interpret its estimate causally.

**Scope:** `fuzzy_rd` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** In a fuzzy design, the paper should state and argue two assumptions: crossing the cutoff affects the outcome only through treatment (exclusion restriction), and it moves treatment in only one direction (monotonicity).

**Why it matters:** A causal reading of the estimate requires both assumptions, so addressing only one is not enough.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the exclusion restriction (crossing the cutoff affects the outcome only through treatment) and monotonicity (no defiers).

- **Pass:** The paper states and argues both the exclusion restriction and monotonicity for its fuzzy design.
- **Flag:** The paper gives a fuzzy-RD estimate a causal interpretation while stating neither exclusion nor monotonicity; state partial satisfaction as a FLAG when only one of the two is addressed.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Fernanda Brollo, Tommaso Nannicini, Roberto Perotti, & Guido Tabellini. (2013). The Political Resource Curse. American Economic Review, 103(5), 1759-1796. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.103.5.1759 - p. 1779
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Brigham Frandsen, & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Randomization Inference in the Regression Discontinuity Design: An Application to Party Advantages in the U.S. Senate. Journal of Causal Inference, 3(1), 1-24. https://doi.org/10.1515/jci-2013-0010 - p. 20

### RDD-IDENT-09 - A politician-characteristic RD must state the extra identifying assumption isolating the characteristic and define the treatment's scope.

**Scope:** `pcrd` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the treatment is a trait of the winning politician, the paper should state the extra assumption that isolates that trait, or define the effect as a bundle, and say which related traits count as treatment.

**Why it matters:** The trait exists before the election and can shape who wins close races, so winners with and without it may differ in other ways; an extra assumption is needed to isolate the trait.

**Check:** Whether the paper acknowledges the compound/post-treatment problem and states the additional identifying assumption (or redefines the estimand as the bundle) and specifies which traits are the treatment.

- **Pass:** The paper names the extra assumption it relies on (the characteristic does not shift the victory margin, or no compensating differential affects the outcome) or explicitly targets the compound treatment, and states which correlated traits are included.
- **Flag:** The paper reports a politician-characteristic effect as if it were a standard RD, without stating the extra assumption or defining the treatment's boundaries.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - John Marshall. (2022). Can Close Election Regression Discontinuity Designs Identify Effects of Winning Politician Characteristics?. American Journal of Political Science, 68(2), 494-510. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12741 - pp. 495, 501

### RDD-IDENT-10 - The paper must not condition its sample or outcome on a post-treatment variable without demonstrating treatment did not affect it.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not limit its sample or define its outcome using something that happened after treatment, such as survival or running again, unless it shows treatment did not affect that variable.

**Why it matters:** Selecting on something the treatment could have changed brings selection back into the comparison.

**Check:** Whether the paper restricts its estimation sample, or defines the outcome, on a variable that could have been affected by treatment, and if so whether it demonstrates no treatment effect on that variable.

- **Pass:** The paper either avoids conditioning the sample/outcome on any post-treatment variable, or shows treatment does not affect the conditioning variable.
- **Flag:** The paper conditions the sample or outcome on a post-treatment variable (e.g. survival, running again, an intermediate outcome) without showing treatment did not affect it.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Taylor C. Boas & F. Daniel Hidalgo. (2011). Controlling the Airwaves: Incumbency Advantage and Community Radio in Brazil. American Journal of Political Science, 55(4), 869-885. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2011.00532.x - p. 876
  - John DiNardo & David Lee. (2004). Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984-2001. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 119(4), 1383-1441. https://doi.org/10.1162/0033553042476189 - p. 1411
  - Riako Granzier, Vincent Pons, & Clémence Tricaud. (2023). Coordination and Bandwagon Effects: How Past Rankings Shape the Behavior of Voters and Candidates. American Economic Journal Applied Economics, 15(4), 177-217. https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20210840 - p. 194

## EST

*Estimation - whether the estimator recovers the target parameter.*

### RDD-EST-01 - The paper's primary RD estimate must not rest on a global high-order (order 4+) polynomial.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper's main estimate should come from a local fit near the cutoff or from a curve of order two or lower fit across the whole score range, not from a high-order polynomial (order four or more); a lone third-order curve is borderline.

**Why it matters:** Such curves fit poorly at the cutoff and give estimates that shift with the chosen order and have unreliable confidence intervals.

**Check:** The estimator behind the paper's headline RD estimate: whether it is a local (bandwidth-restricted) estimator or a global polynomial fit over the full range, and the polynomial order of that global fit.

- **Pass:** The headline estimate comes from a local estimator, or from a global polynomial of order two or lower.
- **Flag:** The headline estimate comes from a global polynomial of order four or higher fit over the full running-variable range.
- **When silent:** PASS
- **Threshold:** cutoff 4; provenance: rule of thumb; borderline band: [3, 4]
- **Inside the band:** Order 3 (the border band) PASSes only if the paper also reports a local-estimator or lower-order specification giving the same conclusion; a lone order-3 global fit is a borderline FLAG. Order 4 and above FLAGs; order 2 or lower, or any local estimator, PASSes.

**Further reading**
  - Andrew Gelman & Guido W. Imbens. (2017). Why High-Order Polynomials Should Not Be Used in Regression Discontinuity Designs. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 37(3), 447-456. https://doi.org/10.1080/07350015.2017.1366909 - pp. 447, 455
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Nicolás Idrobo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2019). A Practical Introduction to Regression Discontinuity Designs. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108684606 - p. 40

## INFER

*Inference - standard errors, tests, and their validity.*

### RDD-INFER-01 - A paper using a data-driven MSE-optimal bandwidth must report robust bias-corrected (or undersmoothed) inference, not conventional CIs.

**Scope:** `local_poly_datadriven` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources) · **Disputed** - Hall (2015) advises reporting the more conservative of robust and conventional standard errors in small samples, endorsing conventional inference contrary to the requirement's exclusion of conventional CIs.

**In plain words:** When the paper picks its bandwidth (the window around the cutoff) with a data-driven rule that balances bias and noise, it should report robust bias-corrected confidence intervals or use a narrower bandwidth, not conventional intervals.

**Why it matters:** That data-driven bandwidth leaves bias in the estimate, so conventional confidence intervals at it are invalid.

**Check:** For a paper using local polynomial estimation with a data-driven bandwidth, whether its confidence intervals are robust bias-corrected (or the bandwidth is undersmoothed below the MSE-optimal rate) rather than conventional intervals at the MSE-optimal bandwidth.

- **Pass:** The paper reports robust bias-corrected confidence intervals, or states it undersmooths the bandwidth for inference.
- **Flag:** The paper forms conventional confidence intervals at a data-driven MSE-optimal bandwidth without bias correction or undersmoothing.
- **When silent:** FLAG
- **Prevalence:** Calonico (2014a) notes the pairing of local-linear estimation with MSE-optimal bandwidths and conventional CIs plausibly affects many published RD studies.

**Further reading**
  - Sebastián Calónico, Matias D. Cattaneo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Robust Nonparametric Confidence Intervals for Regression-Discontinuity Designs. Econometrica, 82(6), 2295-2326. https://doi.org/10.3982/ecta11757 - p. 2295
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Nicolás Idrobo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2019). A Practical Introduction to Regression Discontinuity Designs. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108684606 - p. 67
  - Luke Keele & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Geographic Boundaries as Regression Discontinuities. Political Analysis, 23(1), 127-155. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu014 - p. 139

### RDD-INFER-02 - A paper with grouped/repeated observations must report standard errors that account for within-group correlation (e.g., clustered at the grouping level).

**Scope:** `clustered` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When observations come in groups or repeat, the paper should report standard errors that allow for correlation within groups, for example by clustering at the group level.

**Why it matters:** Treating related observations as independent overstates statistical significance.

**Check:** Whether a paper whose data structure is grouped/repeated reports standard errors clustered at the grouping level. Fired-vs-not is decided from whether the paper declares grouped/repeated observations; a fired trigger with unclustered errors takes verdict_when_silent, an unfired or ambiguous trigger is NA.

- **Pass:** The paper with grouped/repeated observations reports standard errors clustered at the appropriate level.
- **Flag:** The paper declares grouped/repeated observations but reports standard errors that treat them as independent.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - John DiNardo & David Lee. (2004). Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984-2001. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 119(4), 1383-1441. https://doi.org/10.1162/0033553042476189 - p. 1435
  - Andrew Leigh. (2007). Estimating the impact of gubernatorial partisanship on policy settings and economic outcomes: A regression discontinuity approach. European Journal of Political Economy, 24(1), 256-268. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejpoleco.2007.06.003 - p. 276

### RDD-INFER-03 - A discrete-running-variable paper must adjust inference for specification error rather than assume continuous-variable inference holds.

**Scope:** `discrete_rv` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the score takes only a limited set of values (a discrete running variable), the paper should adjust its standard errors for errors in the assumed curve, or acknowledge its reliance on that curve.

**Why it matters:** With a discrete score, the estimate leans on the assumed shape of the curve, so methods built for continuous scores do not simply carry over.

**Check:** For a paper that states its running variable is discrete, whether it adjusts inference for the discreteness (e.g. grouped / specification-error standard errors) or acknowledges the functional-form dependence.

- **Pass:** The paper widens or groups its standard errors for specification error (or otherwise addresses that discreteness forces functional-form reliance).
- **Flag:** The paper has a discrete running variable but applies standard continuous-variable RD inference without acknowledging the specification-error problem.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Sebastián Calónico, Matias D. Cattaneo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Robust Nonparametric Confidence Intervals for Regression-Discontinuity Designs. Econometrica, 82(6), 2295-2326. https://doi.org/10.3982/ecta11757 - p. 2299
  - David S. Lee & Thomas Lemieux. (2010). Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics. Journal of Economic Literature, 48(2), 281-355. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.48.2.281 - p. 340

### RDD-INFER-04 - A geographic RD paper must account for spatial correlation in its inference.

**Scope:** `geographic_rd` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** In a design comparing places on either side of a geographic boundary, the paper's standard errors should account for nearby observations being correlated, for example through clustering or spatial standard errors.

**Why it matters:** Nearby units tend to be alike, so inference that ignores this does not reflect the true uncertainty.

**Check:** For a geographic/boundary RD, whether the paper's inference accounts for spatial correlation among nearby observations.

- **Pass:** The paper reports inference (clustering, spatial standard errors, or an equivalent) that accounts for spatial correlation near the boundary.
- **Flag:** The geographic RD paper reports standard errors that ignore spatial dependence among nearby units.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Luke Keele & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Geographic Boundaries as Regression Discontinuities. Political Analysis, 23(1), 127-155. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu014 - p. 128

## ROBUST

*Robustness - sensitivity, diagnostics, and alternative specifications.*

### RDD-ROBUST-01 - The paper must report its RD estimate at two or more distinct bandwidths.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should report its estimate using at least two different bandwidths, meaning windows of data around the cutoff.

**Why it matters:** The bandwidth drives the estimate, so results at more than one show the finding is not an artifact of a single choice.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports its RD estimate at two or more distinct bandwidths (or window widths).

- **Pass:** The paper reports the RD estimate at two or more distinct bandwidths / window widths.
- **Flag:** The paper reports the estimate at only a single bandwidth with no bandwidth-variation check.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Nicolás Idrobo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2019). A Practical Introduction to Regression Discontinuity Designs. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108684606 - p. 106
  - Andrew B. Hall. (2015). What Happens When Extremists Win Primaries?. American Political Science Review, 109(1), 18-42. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055414000641 - p. 35

### RDD-ROBUST-02 - The paper must report its RD estimate under two or more functional-form specifications.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should report its estimate under at least two shapes for the curve fit to the score, such as two polynomial orders or a local versus whole-range fit.

**Why it matters:** The fitted shape drives the estimate, so the result should hold under more than one.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports its RD estimate under two or more functional-form specifications (e.g. two polynomial orders or a local-vs-parametric comparison).

- **Pass:** The paper reports the estimate under two or more distinct functional-form or polynomial-order specifications.
- **Flag:** The paper reports the estimate under a single functional form with no specification-variation check.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Andrew Gelman & Guido W. Imbens. (2017). Why High-Order Polynomials Should Not Be Used in Regression Discontinuity Designs. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 37(3), 447-456. https://doi.org/10.1080/07350015.2017.1366909 - p. 447
  - Andrew B. Hall. (2015). What Happens When Extremists Win Primaries?. American Political Science Review, 109(1), 18-42. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055414000641 - p. 23

### RDD-ROBUST-03 - The paper must test the running-variable density for a discontinuity at the cutoff.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should test whether units bunch on one side of the cutoff, using a density test such as a McCrary-type test.

**Why it matters:** A sudden pile-up of units on one side of the cutoff is a sign that units sorted themselves around it.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports a test (or diagnostic) of the running-variable density for a discontinuity at the cutoff.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a running-variable density / manipulation test (e.g. a McCrary-type test or an equivalent density-continuity diagnostic) at the cutoff.
- **Flag:** The paper never examines the running-variable density for a discontinuity at the cutoff.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Guido W. Imbens & Thomas Lemieux. (2007). Regression discontinuity designs: A guide to practice. Journal of Econometrics, 142(2), 615-635. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.001 - p. 629
  - Thomas Lemieux & Kevin Milligan. (2007). Incentive effects of social assistance: A regression discontinuity approach. Journal of Econometrics, 142(2), 807-828. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.014 - p. 824
  - Jessica Trounstine. (2011). Evidence of a Local Incumbency Advantage. Legislative Studies Quarterly, 36(2), 255-280. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-9162.2011.00013.x - p. 264

### RDD-ROBUST-04 - The paper must test predetermined covariates for balance / continuity at the cutoff.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should test whether characteristics set before treatment jump at the cutoff, for example by rerunning the analysis with each characteristic as the outcome.

**Why it matters:** If the design is valid, characteristics set before treatment should be balanced at the cutoff.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports balance / continuity tests on predetermined covariates at the cutoff (e.g. re-running the RD with covariates as outcomes).

- **Pass:** The paper reports covariate balance / continuity checks on predetermined characteristics at the cutoff.
- **Flag:** The paper reports no covariate balance or continuity check at the cutoff.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Taylor C. Boas & F. Daniel Hidalgo. (2011). Controlling the Airwaves: Incumbency Advantage and Community Radio in Brazil. American Journal of Political Science, 55(4), 869-885. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2011.00532.x - p. 876
  - Devin Caughey & Jasjeet S. Sekhon. (2011). Elections and the Regression Discontinuity Design: Lessons from Close U.S. House Races, 1942–2008. Political Analysis, 19(4), 385-408. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr032 - p. 388
  - John DiNardo & David Lee. (2004). Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984-2001. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 119(4), 1383-1441. https://doi.org/10.1162/0033553042476189 - p. 1412

### RDD-ROBUST-05 - The paper should report a placebo-cutoff falsification check (RD estimates at cutoff values where no effect is expected).

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should report estimates at fake (placebo) cutoff values, where no effect is expected.

**Why it matters:** A jump should appear only at the true cutoff, so placebo cutoffs help test the design, though they support it rather than settle it.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports RD estimates at artificial / placebo cutoff values away from the true cutoff.

- **Pass:** The paper reports estimates at one or more placebo cutoff values (or placebo points where no effect should appear).
- **Flag:** The paper reports no placebo-cutoff / placebo-point check.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Matias D. Cattaneo, Nicolás Idrobo, & Rocío Titiunik. (2019). A Practical Introduction to Regression Discontinuity Designs. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108684606 - pp. 100-101
  - Thomas Fujiwara. (2015). Voting Technology, Political Responsiveness, and Infant Health: Evidence From Brazil. Econometrica, 83(2), 423-464. https://doi.org/10.3982/ecta11520 - p. 433

### RDD-ROBUST-06 - When interpreting a battery of balance/placebo/outcome tests, the paper should apply a multiple-comparisons correction or report a joint/omnibus test rather than reading individual rejections at face value.

**Scope:** `multiple_tests` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper interprets many balance, placebo, or outcome tests, it should correct for multiple comparisons or report a joint test, rather than reading each significant result on its own.

**Why it matters:** Running many tests will turn up some significant results by chance.

**Check:** For a paper reporting several covariate-balance, placebo, or multiple-outcome tests, whether it applies a multiple-comparisons correction (or a joint test) before reading individual rejections.

- **Pass:** The paper applies a multiple-testing correction or reports a joint test when interpreting its battery of tests.
- **Flag:** The paper reports many separate tests and reads individual significant results at face value without any multiplicity adjustment.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Brandon De La Cuesta & Kosuke Imai. (2016). Misunderstandings About the Regression Discontinuity Design in the Study of Close Elections. Annual Review of Political Science, 19(1), 375-396. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-polisci-032015-010115 - p. 387
  - Andrew C. Eggers, Anthony Fowler, Jens Hainmueller, Andrew B. Hall, & James M. Snyder. (2014). On the Validity of the Regression Discontinuity Design for Estimating Electoral Effects: New Evidence from Over 40,000 Close Races. American Journal of Political Science, 59(1), 259-274. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12127 - p. 263
  - Luke Keele & Rocío Titiunik. (2014). Geographic Boundaries as Regression Discontinuities. Political Analysis, 23(1), 127-155. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu014 - p. 139

## REPORT

*Reporting - what the paper must state for a reader to evaluate it.*

### RDD-REPORT-01 - The paper should interpret its RD estimate as local to the cutoff, not as a population-wide effect.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources) · **Clarity check**

**In plain words:** The paper should describe its estimate as the effect for units near the cutoff (and, in a fuzzy design, for units whose treatment responds to the cutoff), or name the assumption it uses to generalize.

**Why it matters:** The design measures an effect at the cutoff, not an average across the whole population.

**Check:** Whether the paper states that its estimate is local to the cutoff (and, if fuzzy, applies to compliers) rather than presenting it as a general population effect.

- **Pass:** The paper describes its estimand as local to the cutoff, or names the additional assumption it invokes to generalize.
- **Flag:** The paper presents its RD estimate as a population-wide/average effect without noting its locality or any extrapolation assumption.
- **When silent:** FLAG
- **If flagged, the author can fix it by:** State explicitly that the RD estimate is a local effect at the cutoff (for compliers, in a fuzzy design) and does not by itself identify a population-wide average effect; if you generalize beyond the cutoff, name the extra assumption you rely on.

**Further reading**
  - Taylor C. Boas & F. Daniel Hidalgo. (2011). Controlling the Airwaves: Incumbency Advantage and Community Radio in Brazil. American Journal of Political Science, 55(4), 869-885. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2011.00532.x - p. 874
  - Elisabeth R. Gerber & Daniel J. Hopkins. (2011). When Mayors Matter: Estimating the Impact of Mayoral Partisanship on City Policy. American Journal of Political Science, 55(2), 326-339. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00499.x - p. 330

## DATA

*Data - sample construction and measurement.*

### RDD-DATA-01 - A paper with a heaped running variable must run supplementary heaping-specific checks.

**Scope:** `heaped_rv` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When many units share certain score values (heaping), the paper should run extra checks for heaping, such as dropping the heaped values or comparing heaped and other units.

**Why it matters:** When heaping is related to outcomes, standard checks can miss the resulting bias.

**Check:** For a paper whose running variable heaps, whether it reports checks aimed at heaping-induced composition bias (e.g. disaggregated heaped-vs-non-heaped plots, a donut estimate dropping heap points, or covariate tests at heaps).

- **Pass:** The paper reports a heaping-specific diagnostic or remedy beyond the standard density/balance checks.
- **Flag:** The paper's running variable heaps but it reports only standard diagnostics and no heaping-specific check.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alan Barreca, Jason M. Lindo, & Glen R. Waddell. (2011). Heaping-Induced Bias in Regression-Discontinuity Designs. National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w17408
